backup.driveApiKeyHelpAria: How do I get a Drive API key?
backup.driveApiKeyHelpText:
Free, one-time setup, no sign-in required to use it:

1. Go to console.cloud.google.com and create a project (or pick an existing one).
2. APIs & Services → Library → search "Google Drive API" → Enable.
3. APIs & Services → Credentials → Create Credentials → API key.
4. Optional but recommended: restrict the key to the Drive API, and restrict it by HTTP referrer to this app's own address.

Paste the key here. It only ever reads files from a folder you've explicitly shared as "Anyone with the link can view" — it can't write, delete, or see anything else in your Drive.

help.allPlayers.graphNote: Each card shows the player's rating badge and, if they've played this period, how much it moved ("▲ +18" or "▼ −9"). In graph view, players on the live roster show their chart immediately; everyone else collapses to a name and a Show Graph button, so the page stays scannable. The graph itself plots cumulative games played/won/lost over time — smoothed curves, a dot at every real data point, a legend where any line can be shown or hidden (Lost starts hidden), and a separate Rating chart underneath tracking that player's rating over the same period (its own scale, since ratings and game counts aren't comparable numbers).

help.league.exportNote: Export League/Import League share a league file between devices — an imported copy is always read-only, even re-imported back onto the organizer's own device.
help.league.intro: An ongoing, never-ending Skill-Level handicap points ladder for a fixed group of players — pick APA, BCA, VNBA, or TAP as the rating system, and each player's own Skill Level handicaps each match's target so a mismatch still plays close. No server: the organizer exports a league file, everyone else imports it to see standings.
help.league.queue: Queue Mode — Manual leaves every table's next pairing to the organizer. Per-Table Queue gives each table its own line; Per-Room Queue shares one line across every table. Either way, both players from a finished match rotate to the back of the line rather than dropping out, and a confirm dialog (with a sound) proposes the next pairing the moment a table frees up.
help.league.setup: Setup — create a league (8-Ball or 9-Ball), add members from your known players, and set each member's Skill Level (a suggested value is filled in from their app rating, freely editable).
help.league.tables: Tables — set how many physical tables are running; each shows up as its own slot in the Tables grid, and a match scored to its target there finishes and updates standings automatically, on its own board, without affecting any other table's live game.
help.league.teams: Teams — group league members into teams, then assign a team to a table (Per-Table Queue mode) to seed that table's queue with the whole roster in order — a one-tap way to keep a team's players rotating through their table on their own.
help.main.backup: Backup & Transfer — Export All Data downloads one JSON file with everything: the live session, saved player lists, saved rotations, career stats, and ratings. Import Data reads a backup back in — it merges into what's already here rather than overwriting, and adopts the backup as-is only if this device has no players yet. Export for iCloud Sync does the same export, named with today's date, day of the week, and whoever's exporting (e.g. "2026-09-08-Tuesday-Luc.json") so several people syncing the same iCloud Drive folder each get their own file. It downloads the same way any browser download does — silently, to your browser's normal download folder, not necessarily iCloud Drive — so point your browser's download location at a folder inside iCloud Drive (a one-time setting) for it to land there automatically; then use Import Data on your other device and pick any of those files to bring it up to date. Reset All Player Stats and Reset Player Lists live in the All Resets section below, not here.
help.main.currentGame: Current Session — Tournament Setup: Load Setup applies a saved configuration in one tap; Tournament Type is either Race to Wins (set how many wins ends it) or Timed Tournament (set a duration instead); Games Rotation is either Rotate game types automatically or Single Game; Use Q-Score to balance the race shortens the underdog's target based on the rating gap (❓ for the exact math). Current Game: the game type, the target number, and the unit (rack/balls/points — adjustable independently of the game type's usual default, e.g. One Pocket to "1 rack" instead of "8 balls"), plus the Shot Counter. Reset Current Game (clearing the live score without crediting a win) lives in the All Resets section below; Undo Last Win is the − button on a player's card once their game reaches its target.
help.main.gameOrder: Games Rotations — Turn on "Rotate game types automatically" to cycle through a sequence of game rules on their own. Each step in the order is its own rule — game type, target number, and unit (rack/balls/points) — so the same game type can appear twice with different rules (e.g. "8-Ball — 1 rack" then "8-Ball — 3 racks"). The target number and unit are editable right in the list — change either any time without removing and re-adding the step. "Switch every" controls how many games play before advancing. Load Rotation swaps in a saved sequence outright; any new sequence you build is auto-saved as a loadable entry the moment it's set up or played.
help.main.intro: The main page is where every game gets played. Every panel here is collapsed by default with a one-line summary of what's inside — tap the chevron to expand it. The "🎨 Theme" dropdown at the very top switches the whole app's colors and font in one tap and remembers your choice — six dark palettes, two bright/light ones, and two high-contrast pairs (one dark, one light) for maximum legibility.
help.main.players: Players — Add a player by name (auto-capitalized, checked live for a duplicate nickname — the Add button stays disabled until the name is unique). The optional "Starting rating" field lets you seed a brand-new player's rating from a number they've earned elsewhere (another league, another tournament) — it only takes effect for a name that's never been rated on this device before; it's ignored for anyone already tracked. Tap a player's Standby/Playing badge to move them in or out of the current game. The ✕ removes someone from today's roster only — career stats and rating stay on the device; no confirmation if no games have been played yet this session, since there's nothing to lose. Load Player List swaps in players from a saved list (adds anyone missing, never resets what's already there); Export/Import Player Lists use a separate, hand-editable JSON format just for lists.
help.main.ratingsNote: Ratings show as a small badge next to every player's name throughout the app — an Elo-style number (see the Player Stats section below for details). Every player's name is also a shortcut: tap it (the 📊 icon on the roster row) to open their individual stats page.
help.main.recentGames: Recent Games — Every game finished in the last 24 hours, most recent first — a rolling window, not a calendar day, so it keeps building right up until a game finally falls out the far end, even across a race being won and the next one starting fresh. Each winner's rating change from that exact game shows beside their badge; the game that completes a race-to-N gets a gold highlight and its own banner line ("🏆 Alice won the Race to 5 session!").
help.main.resets: All Resets — Every reset button in the app, gathered in one place: Reset Current Game (clears the live score, no win credited), Reset Tournament (offers to save the session first if there are unsaved games, then clears session wins/history and ends any active bracket tournament together), Reset All Players' Official Rating (roster only, back to the default starting rating), and Reset All Player Stats / Reset Player Lists (each backs up first, warns you, then clears — career stats plus the live session, and saved lists, respectively; ratings are never touched). Ending just an in-progress tournament without touching the live session is still on the Tournament page's own Abandon Tournament button. Below a dashed line at the bottom sits 💀 Full Reset — the one button that wipes the entire device back to a brand new install (every player, rating, roster, game, tournament, and setting). It's gated behind two confirmations and downloads a full backup automatically first, but recovering afterward means re-importing that file by hand — it doesn't appear in Recover Data like the resets above.
help.main.scoreboard: Scoreboard — Sits right above the player cards, visible whether Focus Mode is on or off. "Do not record games statistics and players data" stops every save while it's checked — nothing goes into state, career stats, or ratings until you uncheck it; wins still count live on screen for the rest of this browser tab, but none of it survives a reload. Tap + / − on a player's card to track balls/points/racks toward the target. Reaching the target banks a win and starts the next game. Focus Mode hides every other panel down to just the scoreboard — while in it, a small "Players" chevron above the board still lets you flip who's Playing vs Standby without leaving focus; every number on screen also scales up (up to 3x) to stay readable from across the room, shrinking back down on its own once enough players are on screen that the cards get narrower. Whenever Games Rotations is on with 2+ game types, a "Rotation Position" line appears right under the "Now Playing" banner with ◀/▶ buttons - each tap moves the rotation's own games-toward-the-next-switch counter by exactly one game (the same counter a real win advances), so it only actually changes the active game type once enough taps cross a switch-every boundary. No score, win, or ball count is touched - it's purely for correcting the rotation's position by hand if it ever drifts.
help.main.standings: Standings — Live race-to-N progress for teams and individuals this session.
help.main.todaysNotes: Publish Daily Report — A free-text box for anything worth remembering about today's live play; it saves automatically as you type. Copy/Email/Text Report builds a plain-text day report — who played, win/loss and rating movement for each, total games, game types played, a game-by-game breakdown (grouped by matchup — "Luc won 3 games of 8-Ball against Suresh" rather than one line per game) split into earlier-session/current-session, and your notes — ready to paste, email, or send as a text message.

help.playerPage.ratingsAbout: About ratings: every player has an automatic, Elo-style rating (roughly 0–900) inspired by the scale FargoRate publishes — the system behind USA Pool League and most competitive USA leagues. A 100-point gap between two ratings works out to about a 2:1 expected win ratio, doubling every 100 points. New players start at 400, unless a starting rating was given when they were added (see Players, above) — that's a one-time seed for a brand-new name only, not an edit of a rating already being tracked. From there it updates itself after every credited game (main scoreboard or tournament rack) — there's no way to edit an established rating by hand. It's a from-scratch calculation matched to Fargo's published odds, not a copy of Fargo's own (proprietary, globally-recomputed) algorithm. The rating badge follows a player's name everywhere throughout the app.
help.camera.intro: An optional feature: a camera watches the table and automatically selects the correct player on the keypad when they bend over to shoot — either a separate phone mounted over the table, or this tablet's own camera (built-in or USB). It identifies people by clothing and rough body shape, not faces, so it needs a quick one-time "enrollment" per player and a little ongoing upkeep to stay accurate — this section covers all of it.
help.camera.setup: Setup — open the "Visual Scoring" section under the scorecards (or tap "📷 Set Up Camera" at the top, which opens it for you) and choose a path in its "Select Camera" block: a separate phone (works over your local network only, no internet involved) or this tablet's own camera. Same-device mode needs a secure page load (HTTPS, or localhost) to access the camera at all — the setup block tells you if that's not met yet. Once set up, the camera auto-starts minimized into the Visual Scoring section on every future page load — no need to start it by hand again.
help.camera.calibration: Calibrating the table — tells the camera exactly where your table's rails are, so it only counts people actually standing at it, not someone walking past or sitting nearby. Tap "Full Screen" on the camera preview, then either tap the 4 corners yourself (most reliable) or try Auto-Detect (faster, but can mis-detect the felt color if lighting or reflections are tricky). Turn on "Show camera debug info" afterward and check the pink outline it draws actually traces your real table — if it doesn't, redo calibration before trusting anything else.
help.camera.enroll: Enrollment — each unenrolled player shows an "Enroll" button in the roster; tap it to open the camera's player list, where each player has an Identify button (press while they're at the table) and a Shooting button (press while they're down on a shot) — every press adds a sample, at any time, even mid-game. Each player's row also shows a self-check: how often the camera recognizes them from their own samples, who it mixes them up with, and any sample that looks more like someone else, with a button to remove it. The camera recognizes players two ways - clothing colours, and an appearance model trained on thousands of people - and the self-check picks whichever does better on tonight's players. Until a player has 20 samples from those buttons, every point you confirm for them on the keypad also teaches the camera what they currently look like — so select the correct player on the keypad before confirming each point. After that, only the buttons add samples: if a player changes shirts, press Identify and Shooting for them a few times. With a number pad: during play, select a player with their number, then 7 = seen, 8 = shooting, 0 = take back the last one; on the camera's Enroll tab, a player's number = seen, + = shooting, - = take back. Tap the "?" beside any enrolled player's icon for the full explanation in plain terms.
help.camera.scorecardIcons: Scorecard icons — once set up, a small camera icon appears above a player's name on the scorecard whenever the camera has something to say about them: flashing means it's watching them live right now; it stops flashing the instant their shot is confirmed; a "+" means a fresh sample just got captured for them; a "?" means the camera sees someone bent over it can't confidently name, and this is its best guess — tap that player on the keypad to confirm (this also feeds the camera a strong, human-confirmed sample); a small clock means a seated player waiting their turn is still being recognized in the background.
help.camera.unmatchedBanner: "Select player from keypad" banner — appears under the scorecards whenever the camera sees someone shooting it can't identify at all. It clears itself once resolved; tapping the actual shooter on the keypad dismisses it and tells the camera who that was, same effect as the per-player "?" icon above.
help.camera.settings: Tuning settings — Match sensitivity, Consecutive frames, Re-announce after, both Bend angle settings, and Max distance from rail all live in Visual Scoring > Capture Settings (for this tablet's camera or a separate camera phone) and inside the camera's own Settings tab. Every one of them has its own "?" explaining what raising or lowering the number actually does, in plain language — open the right one instead of guessing.
help.camera.troubleshootNote: If recognition seems unreliable: turn on "Show camera debug info" and watch the running log under the checkbox — it shows the actual distance numbers behind every miss, not just pass/fail, which is almost always more useful than guessing at a setting to change. Camera placement matters more than any setting: mount it along one of the table's long sides rather than at one end, since that roughly halves the worst-case difference in how large/clear someone looks depending on where they're standing. All of this — calibration, enrollment, and settings — persists across restarts and travels with Export All Data / Import Data, same as everything else in the app.

help.tournament.format: Format — Double Elimination: lose once, drop to the losers bracket for a second chance; lose twice and you're out. Single Elimination: lose once and you're out — the faster option, no losers bracket or grand final. Round Robin: no elimination at all — everyone plays everyone else once, and whoever has the most match wins once every match is done is champion (a tie is shared by every player at the top).

help.tournament.setup: Setup — pick a format (tap the ❓ next to any format for what it means, then "Yes, this format" to select it), then game type, per-match target, and race-to per match. help.wizard.quickCounterNote: ⏱️ Only a temporary counter — check it on Step 1 and a "▶️ Start Game Now" button appears; tapping it skips the rest of the wizard entirely and drops you into Quick Counter: Focus Mode with a bare point tally — no game type, no target, no rotation, no win/loss detection, and nothing written to storage (state, career stats, ratings, saved lists — all of it, gone the moment you reload). Each card's name is directly editable, every card has its own remove button, scores can go negative, and an "+ Add Player" field sits at the end of the row. If there's a saved player list, a "📋 Load Player List" row also appears — loading one makes the active players match that list exactly, dropping anyone not on it to standby (their data isn't lost — typing their name back in reactivates them) and adding/activating everyone who is. "↺ Reset All to 0" zeroes every card's tally at once, no confirmation needed. Everything needed to add, rename, remove, load, reset, and count is right there in the scoreboard, nothing else to set up.

league.handicapSystemInfoText:
Not sure which to pick? Here's the difference in plain terms.

APA publishes one official nationwide chart — every player's own Skill Level sets a fixed number of games or points to win, the same everywhere. This app already has APA's real chart built in, ready to go.

BCA, VNBA, and TAP don't work that way. Each local league sets its own numbers (or, for TAP, a computer calculates them from recent play) — there's no single official chart to bake in. Pick one of these and add your own league's numbers under Tables → Base Games to Win (and the Skill Level chart, if your league posts one) — the app uses those instead of guessing.

Still deciding? APA is the safe default — it's the only one with real numbers ready from the start.

playerPage.ratingKExplain:
Every player starts at a rating of 400. After each game, the winner's rating goes up and the loser's goes down - but not always by the same amount. Two things decide how much:

1. How surprising the result was. Beating someone rated much higher than you moves your rating more than beating someone you were expected to beat anyway.

2. The "K" number shown here. It controls how fast a rating is allowed to change. New players (under 20 games) use K=24, so their rating catches up to their real skill quickly. Once established, K drops to 8, so one unusual result doesn't swing things too much.

players.cameraInputHelpAria: What does camera player recognition do?
players.cameraInputHelpText:
When this is on, a camera watches the table and automatically confirms or corrects which player is selected on the keypad - either a separate phone/tablet mounted over the table, or this tablet's own camera (USB or built-in). Set either one up from the 📷 Set Up Camera button.

Cross-device setup only works over your local network - no internet or cloud is involved.
players.cameraMatchThresholdHelpText:
How close the camera's best guess has to be to actually count as a match, in the same distance units the debug log shows (e.g. "closest: Elena (1.87, need ≤1.20)"). Lower = stricter (fewer wrong matches, but a real match can get rejected as "too far"); higher = looser (catches real matches more easily, but can start confusing different players for each other).

Turn on "Show camera debug info" and watch the closest-match distance in the log while someone shoots - if it's consistently just a bit over this number, raise it a little. If it's wildly higher (3x or more), the problem is the enrollment, not this setting - re-enroll that player instead.
players.cameraDebounceSecHelpText: Once the camera confirms a player is shooting, it won't send another confirmation for that same player again until this many seconds have passed - so standing at the table and taking several shots in a row doesn't repeatedly re-select them or re-trigger their voice announcement. Lower it if turns are fast; raise it if one visit to the table involves a long multi-shot sequence.
players.cameraDebugEnable: 👁️ Show camera debug info during play
players.cameraDebugEnableHelpAria: What does Show camera debug info do?
players.cameraDebugEnableHelpText: Shows a live status line and a running log (right under this checkbox) of exactly what the camera is detecting - whether it sees a pose at all, upright or bent over, the angle, and the closest enrolled player's name and distance even when nothing officially matches. Turn this on whenever recognition doesn't seem to be working, to see which part is actually failing instead of guessing.
players.cameraVoiceEnableHelpAria: What does Speak player status do?
players.cameraVoiceEnableHelpText: Reads status out loud from this device - "[Name] seen" when the camera recognizes someone standing at the table, and "[Name] shooting" once a shot is confirmed. Useful if you're not looking at the screen. If matching isn't succeeding yet (check the debug log), there's nothing for this to announce, since both phrases only ever fire after a real match. During play, a player the camera switches to isn't spoken (it was constant chatter): only while "Show camera debug info" or Cue debug mode is ticked - and in Straight Pool, a shot the camera is at least 80% sure of (the debug log shows how sure each one was). Pressing Identify or Shooting flashes that player's score card instead: once for seen, twice for shooting.
players.cameraRemoteCalibrateHelpAria: What does Calibrate Table Remotely do?
players.cameraRemoteCalibrateHelpText: Lets you calibrate the table from this screen instead of walking over to the camera phone. Tap the button, and a live still from the camera appears here - tap each corner of the table in the image, one at a time, going around in order, the same as you would on the phone itself. Only works with a separate camera phone (cross-device mode); this tablet's own camera already shows its calibration screen directly.
players.cameraRemoteViewerHelpAria: What does Full Camera Setup (Remote) do?
players.cameraRemoteViewerHelpText: Opens the camera device's full setup screen right here, without walking over to it - table calibration, enrolling players, and recognition settings, all the same controls as standing at the camera phone itself. Tap anything in this window the same way you would on the phone; it happens there for real. Only camera permission has to be granted on the phone itself the first time - everything after that can be done from here.
players.cameraBallTrackingEnable: 🎱 Ball tracking (Straight Pool): auto-credit pocketed balls
players.cameraBallTrackingHelpText: In Straight Pool, the camera counts the balls on the calibrated table between shots. When a ball disappears and stays gone, the selected shooter gets the point automatically; a missing cue ball is announced as a scratch (-1). The camera's own "Ball tracking" setting has to be on as well, and the table has to be calibrated (that's where the pocket positions come from). Nothing is counted while balls are moving, a player is bent over, or a cue or arm is lying on the cloth. If it credits a ball that wasn't pocketed, press - on the keypad; if it misses one, press +. Both corrections teach the camera to be more or less patient. Re-racks and balls that reappear from under a hand are announced, never scored.

players.cameraCueDebugHelpAria: What does Cue debug mode do?
players.cameraCueDebugHelpText: Shows exactly what the camera's cue stick detection is doing. Each time a cue comes out over the table, is put away, or is put down to a player, a line is added to the log under these checkboxes; the camera's video shows the cue drawn in pink with its length and who it was matched to; and - when "Speak player status" is on - you hear "Cue detected on table". When a cue comes out and nobody in view is holding it, the last player the camera saw is set as shooting, and the log says so. It doesn't change what gets detected - turn it off for normal play.

players.cameraMatchSliderHelpText:
How closely someone has to look like an enrolled player before the camera names them as that player.

0 = never names anyone. 3 = the default. 6 = names everyone as their closest enrolled player, however different they look.

Lower = fewer wrong names, but a real player can go unrecognized when the lighting or their clothes look a bit different from when they were enrolled.

Higher = recognizes real players more easily, but starts mixing different players up.

Move it a little at a time: if someone keeps going unrecognized, go up a step; if players get mixed up, go down a step. Re-enrolling a player usually helps more than any setting.
visualScoring.captureSettingsSummary: How the camera decides who's shooting: match sensitivity, timing, bend angles and distance from the table.
visualScoring.captureWaiting: Turn on Camera player recognition and connect the camera phone - its settings show up here once it's connected.
players.cameraConsecutiveFramesHelpAria: What does Consecutive frames required do?
players.cameraConsecutiveFramesHelpText:
How many detection frames in a row have to agree before the camera trusts what it's seeing - a stance change, a stable match, a shot.

Lower = reacts faster, but more likely to be fooled by one bad or blurry frame.

Higher = slower to react, but steadier and less prone to false triggers.

If switching players feels laggy, lower it a bit. If it fires on brief glitches, raise it.
players.cameraBendEnterHelpAria: What does the bent-over enter angle do?
players.cameraBendEnterHelpText:
How many degrees a player's torso has to tip forward from straight up before the camera decides they're bending over to shoot.

Lower = catches a short, shallow bend faster, but can be set off by just leaning in.

Higher = needs a deeper, more obvious bend - fewer false triggers, but can miss a quick, shallow shot. A cue held out over the table counts as shooting whatever this angle reads.
players.cameraBendExitHelpAria: What does the back-to-upright angle do?
players.cameraBendExitHelpText:
How far a player has to straighten back up before the camera considers them upright again.

Keep it smaller than the enter angle - that gap stops the reading flickering back and forth while someone holds roughly the same lean.

Closer to the enter angle = notices standing up sooner, but flickers more. Lower = steadier, but slower to notice.
players.cameraRailDistanceHelpAria: What does Max distance from the rail do?
players.cameraRailDistanceHelpText:
How far from the nearest table edge someone can stand and still count as "at the table". Only used once the table is calibrated.

Lower = stricter - only someone right at the rail counts, but a player standing back to line up a shot can be missed.

Higher = more forgiving, but someone walking past nearby is more likely to count.
players.cameraBallConfirm: Still passes before a pocketed ball counts
players.cameraBallConfirmHelpAria: What does Still passes before a pocketed ball counts do?
players.cameraBallConfirmHelpText:
Ball tracking only: how many still looks at the table in a row (about one a second) have to agree a ball is gone before it's credited.

Lower = credits faster, but a ball briefly hidden under a hand or glare is more likely to be counted as pocketed.

Higher = slower, steadier. The keypad adjusts this on its own: a - right after an automatic credit raises it, a + the camera missed lowers it.
players.cameraCueDetectionHelpAria: What does Cue stick detection do?
players.cameraCueDetectionHelpText:
Looks for a cue stick held out over the calibrated table. A player at the table with their cue over the cloth is taking a shot - this counts even when the camera can't see them bend over.

If a player drops out of view right next to the table, they're assumed still there, and the next cue that comes out is credited to them. When nobody can be named at all, the last player the camera saw in the last 2 minutes is set as shooting.

Needs the table to be calibrated.
players.cameraEnrollHelpText:
Enrolling a player teaches the camera what they look like right now - their clothes, not their face - so it can recognize them automatically while you play. Tap Enroll to open the camera's player list, where every player has two buttons: Identify - press it while they're at the table, and the camera learns what they look like (clothing colors and rough body shape) and where they stand; Shooting - press it while they're down on a shot, and it also learns how they shoot. Every press adds a sample - as many as you like, at any time, even mid-game.

Until a player has 20 samples from those buttons, every point you confirm for them on the keypad also adds what the camera is currently seeing as a fresh sample - so it keeps up with a shirt change or a shift in lighting. For that, the game manager needs to select the correct player on the keypad before confirming each point - ideally every shot. Once a player has 20 button samples, only the buttons add more (by then the camera's own guesses could teach it a mistake) - so if they change shirts, press Identify and Shooting for them a few times.

The camera's player list also runs a self-check for every player: how often it recognizes them from their own samples, who it mixes them up with, and any sample that looks more like someone else - with a button to remove it. Two players dressed alike are named only when the camera is sure. It recognizes players two ways - clothing colours, and an appearance model trained on thousands of people - and uses whichever the self-check says does better.

tournament.formatDouble:
Winners & Losers Brackets: lose once, drop to the losers bracket for a second chance; lose twice and you're out.

Fairer than single elimination since one bad game doesn't end your tournament — but it takes longer to play out.
tournament.formatRoundRobin:
No elimination — every player faces every other player once.

Whoever has the most match wins when it's all done is champion (ties share the win). Best for a casual group where everyone should get equal games in.
tournament.formatSingle:
Only winners advance: lose once and you're out.

The fastest format — best for a quick knockout when there isn't time for a longer event.
tournament.formatSwiss:
A proper non-elimination format where everyone plays a fixed number of rounds (e.g., 4 or 5), drawn each time against opponents with identical win-loss records.

Once those scheduled rounds wrap up, whoever has bagged the most match victories takes the crown!

keypad.speechHelpText:
🔊 When this is on, the app speaks back out loud whenever you use the keypad (number keys 1-9, Enter) to switch players, and when + or - just gives someone the lead — handy for playing without having to look at the screen.

Switching to a new player (keypad, or a direct tap on their card): "[Previous player], total [count] points" (if someone was already selected), then "[New player] Playing, [count] points" — adding ", Leader" if that player is already ahead.

If a point just put someone in the lead: "[Name] takes the lead" — only on that transition, not on every point while already ahead.

A direct +/- tap on a player's own card also selects that player (same as tapping their name/score) and always speaks the change: "plus/minus [count] point" if they were already the one selected, or "[Name] plus/minus [count] point" if the tap is what just switched the selection to them. For rack-unit games (8-Ball, 9-Ball, etc.), a + that reaches the target still says "[Name] won the game" instead - but only on that same switch, staying silent if the winner was already selected.

The "Voice" dropdown only ever lists the specific voices actually installed on this device (checked live) - Ava, Allison, Reed, Rocko, Evan, Nathan, Samantha, Zoe, Serena, Eddy, Flo, Grandma, Grandpa, Sandy, Shelley, Daniel, Moira, Karen, Rishi, or Tessa, whichever of those are available - falling back to Siri (the device's own best default voice) if none of them are.
